title: External sandboxes for coding agents
summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

title: What We’ve Learned Building Proactive Agents
summary: Proactive agents work toward goals in the background and check in when they need you. What we've learned about memory and UX from building GTM Agent and Robin.
story_key: story|title:what we ve learned building proactive agents
content_excerpt: Think about how you work with a new hire. In their first week, you give them small, well-scoped tasks, like triaging a bug report or updating a doc. Soon you're giving them bigger tasks, and eventually you're handing them a lofty goal and letting them figure out how to tackle it. They still come to you with clarifying questions or review requests, just less often over time. Agents have gotten good enough that you can onboard them the same way, and like a good new hire, they're turning into proactive problem solvers. Personal agents like Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI's dots popularized proactive agents, which run in the background and work toward larger goals instead of waiting for a prompt. Hone puts it most directly, describing its Engines as AI that is "assigned goals rather than tasks." Goals let these agents take on harder problems that play out over days or weeks. A proactive agent still checks in with you when it's unsure what you want or needs your sign-off before something goes out. When your direct reports get really good at their jobs, you might find that you've become the bottleneck, and the same is true for agents. As they take on more goals, your attention becomes the scarce resource. We think two things are essential to building proactive agents that use it well: memory and UX. A proactive agent responds to events in its environment, which come from three places: The examples throughout come from two proactive agents we run internally at LangChain: These agents operate on all three types of triggers. A few examples: Robin's reviews start from a real-world event, a newly opened pull request, and GTM Agent's daily brief runs on a schedule it created itself after a user requests one. We built both agents on Managed Deep Agents , where more than 70% of runs now come from schedules rather than an ad hoc human prompt. A proactive agent decides for itself when to come to you, and each check-in costs you some attention. It has to be proactive without being annoying . For an executive assistant agent that watches your inbox, that means flagging the message from your boss about tomorrow's launch without also flagging every newsletter. The agent can only tell the two apart if it knows what matters to you, and that knowledge comes from memory . Memory is the information an agent learns over time. title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
summary: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

story_key: story|title:branch sync serve what our lakebase hackathon taught us about building on lakeba
content_excerpt: A field guide to Lakebase branching, reverse ETL, and real-time serving, told through eleven customer projects We run these hackathons for a simple reason: the fastest way to learn a product is to build something with it. Each one starts with an enablement session where teams learn the product and where it’s headed on the roadmap. Then the building starts. Teams work together for about a week and submit a project, and the strongest solutions earn prizes. This time, we opened the hackathon to a much wider group of customers than ever before, and the product in the spotlight was Databricks Lakebase . Lakebase is fully managed Postgres, so any developer who has written a SQL query or used an ORM can start building right away. What makes it different is what sits underneath. Storage is separated from compute, and the database lives next to your lakehouse data under the same Unity Catalog governance. That opens up three things a typical Postgres database can’t do as easily: Those map to the two tracks we ran. Track 1 focused on branching and building applications. Track 2 focused on syncing and serving. Underneath both, Unity Catalog governs who can see what, whether the data is being queried in a notebook or read by a production app. Who it’s for: application developers. These are the engineers who build the apps , APIs, and agents that run on operational data, and who have usually had to choose between a slow, shared staging database and an expensive copy for every developer. Branching removes that tradeoff. Every Lakebase project starts with a production branch, and you can create child branches from it for development, testing, or experiments. Because branches use copy-on-write, a branch of a large database is ready in seconds, and only the changes take up new storage. Teams in this track used Genie Code to build their apps and treated branches as cheap, disposable copies of production. Lyft took on a problem that’s growing as AI agents start acting on production data: agents that issue refunds, cancel bookings, or close tickets without knowing the business rules that live inside the database as triggers. Their project, Jevons Search, gives the agent a Lakebase branch to work on. For each batch of support tickets, the agent forks a copy-on-write branch of production in about six seconds, applies its actions, reads back what the database actually did, and adjusts. title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
summary: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.

title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

content_excerpt: We brought MiniMax H3-Image to NVIDIA Vera Rubin with vLLM-Omni. On four GPUs, native 4096×4096 generation reaches 0.87 seconds median in our short-prompt serving benchmark. A separate throughput configuration delivers 6,115 images/hour , projecting to 146,755 images/day . At USD 0.06879 per image , using MiniMax's official Standard 4K API pricing example before launch discounts as an assumed sale price, peak throughput projects to USD 105.16/GPU/hour in gross revenue at full billable utilization, or USD 78.87/GPU/hour at 75%. These estimates are before operating costs; the daily capacity is an extrapolation of the measured rate. H3-Image is an open-weight model for text-to-image generation and image editing. One checkpoint handles both tasks in six sampling steps, generates native high-resolution images without an upscaler, and supports up to 16 reference images. We bring H3-Image to consumer and data-center GPUs , spanning NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Moore Threads (MUSA) , as well as Huawei Ascend NPUs . Oil-paint strokes, a multi-view camera drawing, Japanese poster lettering and tiny words on a rice grain reveal what a smaller image can lose. A game environment adds weathered stone and reflected light. Each uses one H3-Image-generated 4K image, resized to 1K and 2K with its aspect ratio preserved, so composition stays fixed. The two API modes are straightforward: Text-to-Image takes a prompt; Image Edit takes a prompt and one or more reference images. Our main comparisons use 2K (2048×2048) and 4K (4096×4096) output, with one image returned per request. The prompts and reference files stay fixed across machines.   • Fixed an interactive --chrome session giving no reason for starting without Claude in Chrome when your organization's policy turns it off: a line now says so
  • Fixed the /rewind list on network paths and hung folders: it named every tracked file as changed, was slow to show labels, and showed none at all when a file read never returned
  • Fixed --debug and --debug-file replacing a file named latest in the debug log's folder
  • Fixed a timed-out feedback send being reported as too large; it now says the request timed out
  • Fixed screen reader mode cutting off an announcement when the system clock moved forward while it was being read
  • Fixed screen reader mode dropping dictated or pasted text, and emoji, typed into an answer to a question or permission prompt
  • Fixed the name label under permission and plan dialogs hiding part of some agent names
  • Fixed a case where pressing Ctrl+C just as claude update finished removed the claude command
  • Fixed the fullscreen header naming the session's effort level for a viewed subagent on a different model, which that subagent doesn't use
  • Fixed the model picker and /model showing a picked effort level that CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL overrides
  • Fixed the tip after a slow worktree creation suggesting a sparsePaths list without .claude, which left worktrees without your project settings and rules
  • Fixed the newest model's highlight missing from the /model picker
  • Fixed /upgrade and Ctrl+clicked links in fullscreen failing silently when no browser can open: the address is now shown
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's JSON logs escaping newlines and other control characters in a message twice
  • Fixed terminal control sequences in a subagent's message taking effect instead of showing as plain text when the message is expanded
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome setup saying /chrome finishes the connection; it now tells you to restart with claude --chrome
  • Fixed the Option-key hint appearing while typing ø or π inside words on Danish, Norwegian, Faroese and Greek keyboard layouts
  • Fixed a Claude Desktop session getting stuck as busy after another of your sessions sent it the same message twice or many messages at once
  • Fixed long tool results staying on disk after a session run with --no-session-persistence; they are now removed on normal exit, Ctrl+C or SIGTERM
  • Fixed PreCompact, PostCompact and post-compaction SessionStart hooks not receiving agent_id and agent_type when a subagent compacts
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping messages from the saved transcript when another process rewrote the file while it was being trimmed
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice repeating or not showing past the weekly Fable limit when Claude Code made a quick side request on a smaller model, such as naming the session
  • Fixed Fable's weekly limit showing no reset time and no options menu in the terminal
  • Fixed a wait chosen in the usage limit menu silently moving to a later reset when its request was refused; the menu now opens
  • Fixed the spend limit menu offering a lower limit when your current limit couldn't be loaded
  • Fixed /usage hiding limit bars for setup tokens and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: it keeps the session and weekly bars and says why the rest are missing
  • Fixed /usage showing a whole-session percentage beside a subagent type's name, and saying sessions ran 8 hours when it only counts hours with requests
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions showing as disconnected for a minute or more after a network change such as switching Wi-Fi or reconnecting a VPN
  • Fixed Remote Control showing nothing while Claude Code asks whether to use usage credits: the question now also shows in the Claude app
  • Fixed Remote Control showing a session as running while it waited on a permission prompt that can only be answered in the terminal
  • Remote Control: Fixed claude remote-control reconnecting as a new computer when restarted in the same folder more than 4 hours after it stopped; it now keeps its identity for up to 30 days
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions left running at shutdown, and finished sessions holding their slot, when the disk stops responding
  • Remote Control: Fixed other devices and phone notifications not showing what Claude is asking permission for when DISABLE_TELEMETRY or DO_NOT_TRACK is set
  • Remote Control: Fixed the host exiting, or stopping reading a session's output, in verbose or debug mode when a tool call's command was a number, boolean or object
  • Remote Control: Fixed a host that could stall after sessions failed to start in folders on a filesystem that had stopped responding
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions from the desktop app showing as idle on your phone while background subagents were still running
  • Fixed the Agent SDK's managedSettings ignoring the Remote Control, agent view, Workflows and Artifact off switches
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry export failing silently when an otlp exporter had an endpoint but no OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL: it now defaults to http/protobuf
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry export to the default localhost:4318 endpoint going through a configured proxy
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping all of that variable's attributes from the OpenTelemetry resource; the others are now kept, and /status names the one left off
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry user_prompt events and interaction spans recording a background agent's reply when OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=0
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports failing when a proxy took over 10 seconds to reach the collector; it now has 25 seconds, also the most that OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT can allow (previously 30)
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry agent.name showing a user-defined subagent's name instead of custom when an official plugin's skill launched it
  • Fixed claude agents showing a status from an earlier turn after a session resumes
  • Fixed read-only git commands needing approval, or being refused under claude -p, when CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB is set on Linux
  • Fixed claude agents losing a typed prompt: Esc now needs a second press to clear it, and ctrl+y restores it
  • Fixed the move-to-background key doing nothing in claude attach and claude agents sessions; to detach with Ctrl+B d, press d within 800 ms of Ctrl+B
  • Fixed background sessions ignoring a DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING set only in your shell when the background service started without it
  • Fixed false "needs input" notifications in claude agents after replying to a blocked session, and repeated ones after a background turn ended with no text and only basic tools such as Bash or Read
  • Fixed claude -p silently using another model in text output when settings block the requested one; it now warns on stderr
  • Fixed claude -p printing notes about deniedModels and availableModels entries on every run; /status and claude doctor still list them
  • Windows: Fixed some file-reading Bash commands running without a permission prompt when given a wildcard or a list of files
  • Windows: Fixed Claude Code running a .cmd or .bat wrapper found beside a program's .exe in the same PATH folder (a git.cmd next to git.exe, say); it now runs the .exe, as cmd.exe would
  • Windows: Fixed shell commands failing with "Working directory was deleted" on drives where a folder's real path can't be resolved
  • Fixed a cloud session's history becoming unreadable if its machine stopped just after the history was rewritten
  • Fixed scheduled tasks from an ended session sometimes not running after another session in the same folder used /clear, /resume or /branch
  • Fixed an approved plan being answered with "You are not in plan mode" when the approval arrived after the session's process had restarted, in cloud, self-hosted runner and SDK sessions
  • Cloud sessions: Fixed an answer to Claude's question being lost after a restart in a long conversation
  • Fixed a message dropping out of a cloud session's conversation when the session restarted before Claude replied
  • Cloud sessions: Fixed Claude saying an attached image is missing when the message names its file
  • Fixed a resumed cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when files arrived right after a chat's first reply
  • Fixed streamed replies in cloud sessions missing text from the middle when the session's container shut down partway through a reply
  • Fixed skill files sent from Cowork cloud sessions sometimes failing to upload on the first try
  • Self-hosted runner: Reverted the exit code of an on-demand runner whose work order was superseded to 1; 2.1.321 and 2.1.322 had changed it to 0
  • Improved sign-in errors in /login and claude setup-token for a rejected, unreachable or timed-out request: they now say what happened and what to check
  • Improved Bash permission checks so the same command more reliably gets the same answer on a slow or busy machine
  • Improved Bash permission checks: some commands that could run differently from how they were checked now ask for permission
  • Improved /mcp to show how many of a server's tools were left out because the API would reject their input schema, and why
  • Improved the "Not now" choice when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session: it now says when they load
  • Improved the error for an MCP tool call whose connector ID is mistyped by a character or two: for a server that the host application registered, it now names the tool to call
  • Improved Claude Desktop and cloud sessions for claude.ai accounts with more than 2,000 plugins turned on: a shorter wait at startup, and Claude can now say why plugins are missing
  • Improved memory use with many subagents: a finished subagent's transcript is freed sooner instead of staying in memory while later subagents run
  • Improved installing with the install script: the latest version is no longer downloaded twice
  • Improved WebFetch speed and memory use on deeply nested pages
  • Improved the cleanupPeriodDays cleanup to count folders it can't read as errors
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's /v1/models to state max_input_tokens for models whose context window is certain on every upstream
  • Improved ToolSearch to say when a tool Claude searched for by its short name is already available, instead of only reporting no match
  • Improved start-up on Linux when /home is an autofs map: Claude Code no longer looks up files in /home itself. Set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTOMOUNT_ROOTS for a map root deeper than one folder below /
  • Improved the Fable limit message in -p, SDK, IDE and cloud sessions: it now says when the limit resets, along with how to continue
  • Changed /security-review to ask before Claude runs it, and skills' inline git commands to stop in bare-repository worktrees and similar folders until you allow them, outside auto mode and bypass
  • Changed how many messages each of your sessions on the same machine can send the others without a prompt from you, from about 20 to 100,000
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 20 to 100,000
  • Changed organization settings and policy requests to no longer use a proxy set only by ALL_PROXY; set HTTPS_PROXY if your network needs a proxy for them
  • Changed the context window assumed for a model ID that Claude Code doesn't recognize from 200K to 1M; use /autocompact to compact earlier, or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 to keep 200K
  • Changed sessions on other vendors' models with a smaller window: once full, they can fail every turn until /clear, so set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 before they fill
  • Changed Claude Code's own ripgrep and most internal git commands to run without most of its sign-in tokens and API keys, so a credential helper or hook under such a git command no longer finds them
  • Changed MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1 to run the v2 MCP client in a compatibility mode (earlier handshake, relaxed OAuth sign-in checks), because the v1 MCP client is removed
  • Changed the tool Claude uses to finish an MCP server sign-in so that it asks you to confirm, even in bypass and auto modes; where nobody can be asked, such as in dontAsk mode, use /mcp
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a session at a connector's approval prompt or sign-in inside a running tool to be released as paused at the idle or lifetime limit; a late answer resumes from a fresh clone
  • Changed artifact updates to ask first, even under an allow rule, when people outside your organization can see the artifact or Claude can't check who can
  • Changed glab config set without --global or --host, and glab config edit --local, to fail read-only inside the Bash sandbox; run them outside it
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on macOS, Linux and WSL to ignore write access granted through a symlink in a writable folder that leads elsewhere or to a missing path; grant the real path instead
  • Changed "don't ask again" so an allow rule that looks like it holds a secret, or would be saved to a settings.local.json that git tracks, lasts for the session only and isn't saved
  • Changed the sandbox on macOS and Linux: git worktree add, move and remove now fail read-only, as do commits in a worktree the session wasn't started in or given, even one inside the project
  • Changed start-up to stop when a --settings file isn't valid JSON and has a sandbox key, even one that turns the sandbox off
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails with an error after a PreToolUse hook returned "allow": Claude Code now decides the call as if no hook had answered
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails on input that a PermissionRequest hook rewrote: Claude Code now asks again, or refuses the call where nobody can answer
  • Changed the GitLab merge request badge to show only for the repository a sandboxed session opened in
  • Changed the claude mcp add --help example to a local command
  • Changed mods: a *, namespace or negated hook on engine.create now only observes. To add or withhold a $ noun, hook engine.create by name
  • Changed claude plugin validate to fail a mod whose engine.create hook isn't written in the one accepted form; installed mods keep loading
  • Changed marketplace and plugin installs to fail when a git submodule isn't on the commit its repository records
  • Changed project (.mcp.json) MCP server approvals to match the server's exact name; an approval entry written in another spelling now asks again
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false and VS Code sessions in an untrusted folder: the repository's settings can no longer disable your hooks or turn plugins on or off
  • Changed tool.list plugin hooks so the tools they add or remove apply to the model and every agent
  • Changed claude plugin install and /plugin to show a warning instead of success when a plugin's install command writes to stderr
  • Changed claude.ai chats and Cowork tasks to check a plugin file for secret keys before sending it, and to ask first if it may hold one
  • Changed claude rm and the agents view to say a session is removed from the list, not deleted; claude rm help says the conversation is kept and claude --resume lists it
  • Changed /stickers to say that the sticker pack is all claimed for now, instead of opening a page in the browser
  • Changed a managed settings policyHelper to no longer take environment variables from user or --settings files; set what it needs in managed env or the launching shell
  • Changed a /skill or @file typed between two files picked in claude.ai or the desktop app, or after a picked file and a link, to no longer take effect
  • Changed split-pane agent teammates to check that requests come from their team lead: one that outlives its lead has its asks refused, and plan approvals must be re-sent after /clear or /resume
  • Changed worktree creation to refuse checkouts whose .git folders are links or hold hard links, such as git-new-workdir layouts and cp -al copies; use a plain clone
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a forked skill or a workflow agent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed browser tool calls (Claude in Chrome, the desktop browser pane) to refuse some escaped or JSON-text inputs and tell Claude how to respell them
  • Changed workflows so that a prompt an app marks as not typed no longer reaches their agents as your request
  • Changed computer use on macOS to refuse key chords that hold Space with Control or Option, and more system shortcuts that need your grant
  • Changed first-run setup in Terminal.app to name the "Use Option as Meta key" setting, what Option stops typing, and how to undo it before you agree
  • Changed the maximum of CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS from 64000 to 300000
  • Changed workflows in the desktop app's Code tab to pause at a usage limit and continue after it resets
  • Changed the spend limit and 1M context errors, and /usage-credits, in cloud sessions and under Remote Control: they no longer give a web address
  • Changed which MCP servers are reported by name in OpenTelemetry exports to follow the current connector directory
  • Changed /logout in a background session, which had no effect: it now signs out every session on the computer, deletes stored MCP logins and plugin secrets, and ends the session, as in a terminal
  • macOS: Changed the Bash sandbox so lsof and similar tools may show less about processes a command did not start
  • Changed cloud scheduled tasks: a PostToolUse hook from your own settings can no longer replace the plan in ExitPlanMode's result
  • Changed CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE in Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions to stop applying to auto-memory extraction and, in some sessions, to /btw; the main conversation still follows it
  • Removed the subagentStatusLine setting: subagent rows always use the default look, and settings files that still hold the key load as before
  • Deprecated a plugin's agent setting: it still applies, and now warns at startup, in claude plugin list and in claude plugin validate
  • [VSCode] Added a Claude Code trust prompt before the first session in a folder you haven't trusted; declining leaves the folder's settings and MCP servers unused
  • [VSCode] Added the live output of a running Bash or PowerShell command to the chat, under the command's card
  • [VSCode] Fixed a response that was discarded because its tool call could not be parsed still showing after Claude retried
  • [VSCode] Fixed a queued message missing from a conversation or fork when it directly followed a compaction summary
  • [VSCode] Fixed the "Buy usage credits on claude.ai" button counting as agreement to pay for Fable while usage credits were off
  • [VSCode] Fixed the "extensions want to relaunch the terminal" warning coming back on open terminals after every window reload or restart
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Couldn't load this conversation's saved history" appearing in a new chat whose Claude process had restarted before the first prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen showing the login choices again after a pasted code; it now shows "Signing in…" until the sign-in finishes
  • [VSCode] Fixed the "You've hit your Fable limit" line staying in the VS Code and JetBrains panels after you pick another model
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Fable usage warning in the VS Code and JetBrains panels naming usage credits when they're off or used up
  • [VSCode] Fixed the diff tab not opening for multi-line edits on files with CRLF line endings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation continuing to record after switching sessions
  • [VSCode] Improved sign-in errors behind TLS-inspecting proxies: a certificate failure now says what to do, as the terminal does
  • [VSCode] Changed opening a Claude Code on the web session in a folder where Claude Code's sandbox is on: the extension no longer switches to the session's branch for you, and the dialog says why
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the message when a file fails to upload to a cloud or Remote Control session: it now gives the reason, such as too many pages, a password or a time-out
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved adding a repository Claude can't access to a cloud session: a short message and a Reconnect GitHub button replace the long error
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed self-hosted sessions staying on "Starting Claude Code" after it had started, when you reopened a paused session without sending a message
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed a paused session in a self-hosted environment sometimes still showing "Sending" and a Stop button under the "Session paused" banner
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed pull request updates from GitHub Enterprise Server linking to github.com in cloud sessions; new updates link to your own server
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the message when some network secrets can't be added to a new cloud environment: it lists each host, says why where it can, and stays until you dismiss it
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed very large GitHub Actions job logs and run log archives failing to download or being cut off in cloud sessions
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the new-session repository picker when GitHub single sign-on hides organizations: it now says so even with other repositories listed, and links to reconnect GitHub
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions started from the iOS app with a repository not getting a branch of their own
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an open cloud or Remote Control session's page staying "Disconnected" after a few minutes of failed connections; it now tries to reconnect by itself
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed Try again on an open cloud or Remote Control session's "Connection lost" card sending "Try again" as your message; it now tries to reconnect instead
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed the Stop button disappearing from a cloud session five minutes into a reply that had shown nothing yet while Claude was still working
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an approval prompt sometimes disappearing from a tab left open after a self-hosted runner released the session while it waited for your answer
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a failure notification when a scheduled task's run can't start because its settings require a sandbox that isn't available where it runs
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the Git providers page when your GitHub sign-in has expired: it now asks you to reconnect instead of silently hiding organizations you can link
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed removing a repository from a scheduled task silently moving its GitHub trigger to another repository; Save now waits until you pick one

  • [Claude Code on the web] Added the No repository option to the repository picker for new sessions on a self-hosted environment
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a warning to a cloud session's Delete dialog when deleting it will pause scheduled tasks that run in that session
  • [Remote Control] Fixed your own session saying its environment was deleted when you deleted nothing; it now says your computer is no longer connected
  • [Remote Control] Fixed some sessions still showing as running in the session list after the computer disconnected before Claude started; they now show an error mark or as idle
